# Data Quality Scoring {#sec-quality-scoring}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

A validation report answers detailed questions: which checks failed, on how many rows, and at what
severity. It does not directly answer the question a manager or a dashboard usually asks first,
which is how healthy the data is overall and where it is weakest. Data quality scoring answers that.
It combines the step results into a few scores, one for each of several quality dimensions and one
overall, so you can describe a table's condition with a number and track it over time.

The idea is that different checks measure different aspects of quality. A null check measures
completeness, a set membership check measures validity, and a duplicate check measures uniqueness.
Grouping checks by what they measure turns a long report into a short summary. This chapter covers
the six dimensions Pointblank uses, how each check is assigned to one, and the methods that give you
the per-dimension scores, the overall health score, a visual scorecard, and an assertion for
enforcing minimum scores.

We use `game_revenue` and a plan whose checks cover three dimensions. A couple of the checks have
failures, so the scores are not all 100.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")

validation = (
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue, tbl_name="game_revenue")
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id", dimension="completeness")
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="session_id", dimension="completeness")
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="item_type", set=["iap", "ad"], dimension="validity")
    .col_vals_lt(columns="session_duration", value=40, dimension="validity")
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["session_id", "time"], dimension="uniqueness")
    .interrogate()
)
```

The `dimension=` argument on each step assigns it to a quality dimension, and the scores are grouped
by these assignments.

## The six quality dimensions

Pointblank uses six dimensions of data quality. Completeness is about whether required values are
present, and null checks, `rows_complete()`, and most of the missing-value checks from
@sec-missing-data count toward it. Validity is about whether values have an allowed form, which
covers the comparison, range, set, pattern, and format checks, along with `col_vals_expr()` and the
schema checks. Uniqueness is about unwanted duplicates, which `rows_distinct()` measures.
Consistency is about related values agreeing with each other, and `conjointly()`,
`col_missing_consistent()`, `col_vals_in_table()`, and `tbl_match()` count toward it. Timeliness is
about whether the data is recent, which `data_freshness()` measures. Volume is about whether the
table is the right size, which `row_count_match()` and `col_count_match()` measure.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where the six dimensions come from

These dimensions are not a Pointblank invention. Most of them (completeness, validity, uniqueness,
consistency, and timeliness) appear in data quality frameworks such as the one published by DAMA,
and you will see the same names in many data governance tools. Using familiar names means a
scorecard makes sense to people who already work with these frameworks.
:::

You can set a step's dimension with the `dimension=` argument, as the plan above does, or leave it
out and let Pointblank pick one based on the kind of check. For example, it assigns a null check to
completeness and a distinctness check to uniqueness.

```{python}
inferred = (
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id")
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["session_id", "time"])
    .interrogate()
)

inferred.get_dimension_scores()
```

Without any `dimension=` arguments, the null check is scored under completeness and the distinctness
check under uniqueness. Setting the dimension yourself is useful when you want a check counted under
a different dimension than its default, or when you want the plan to state it explicitly. If you
want to change the default for a kind of check across all your plans, the `dimension_map=` setting
in `pb.config()` does that. For example, `pb.config(dimension_map={"col_vals_lt": "consistency"})`
would score every `col_vals_lt()` step under consistency.

A dimension only appears in the scores if at least one step measures it. A plan with only null and
set checks covers completeness and validity, so the other four dimensions are missing from the
result entirely. They are not reported as 100 or as 0. Adding volume checks, such as confirming that
the table has 2,000 rows and 11 columns, adds volume to the scores.

```{python}
scored = (
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue)
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id", dimension="completeness")
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="item_type", set=["iap", "ad"], dimension="validity")
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["session_id", "time"], dimension="uniqueness")
    .row_count_match(count=2000, dimension="volume")
    .col_count_match(count=11, dimension="volume")
    .interrogate()
)

scored.get_dimension_scores()
```

Four dimensions now have scores. Volume is 100 because both count checks passed, and consistency and
timeliness are still missing because no step measured them. This makes sense: if no check looked at
a dimension, there is nothing to score, and reporting it as 100 would suggest the data had been
checked when it had not. It also means your scores only cover what your plan checks, so a dimension
you care about needs at least one check assigned to it.

## Dimension scores

The `get_dimension_scores()` method returns a dictionary of scores from 0 to 100. A dimension's
score is the percentage of its test units that passed, counted across every step assigned to it.
So a step that checks more data has more influence on the score than a step that checks less.

```{python}
validation.get_dimension_scores()
```

Completeness is 100, because both null checks passed on every row. Uniqueness is 98.9, because 22
of the 2,000 rows share a session and timestamp. Validity is 98.15, and this number shows how the
counting works. The item type check passed on all 2,000 rows and the session duration check failed
on 74, so validity is 3,926 passing test units out of 4,000. It is not the average of the two
steps' pass rates, and it is not a count of how many steps passed.

## The overall health score

The `get_health_score()` method reduces the whole plan to a single number.

```{python}
validation.get_health_score()
```

The score of 99.04 is the percentage of all test units that passed across every step: 9,904 out of
10,000. Steps with more test units count for more. This is the number to track from run to run,
since a drop is an early sign that quality is slipping somewhere. If some dimensions matter more to
you than others, the `dimension_weights=` setting in `pb.config()` gives them more influence on the
overall score.

```{python}
pb.config(dimension_weights={"completeness": 2.0, "validity": 1.0, "uniqueness": 1.0})
weighted_health = validation.get_health_score()

pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
weighted_health
```

With completeness counted double, the overall score goes up to 99.31. The weight applies to test
units, so completeness now counts as 8,000 test units instead of 4,000, and all 8,000 passed. That
gives 13,904 passing out of 14,000. The score goes up because completeness is the strongest
dimension here. The second `pb.config()` call puts this chapter's display settings back and clears
the weights, since any setting you leave out goes back to its default. These settings are global,
so it is a good idea to reset them after a one-off change like this.

## The scorecard

Numbers work well for a pipeline, but a person reviewing quality usually wants something visual. The
`get_scorecard()` method returns a Great Tables object that shows the overall health score along
with the score for each dimension.

```{python}
validation.get_scorecard()
```

The scorecard shows the same figures we computed above, in a compact format that works well on a
dashboard or in a report for stakeholders. Because it is a Great Tables object, you can export it the
same way as the validation report, with `write_raw_html()` for an HTML file or `save()` for an image.
The tabular report of @sec-reports-extracts lists every check, while the scorecard gives the summary
a non-technical reader is more likely to want.

## Requiring minimum scores

Scores are also useful in automation. The `assert_dimension_scores()` method takes a dictionary of
minimum scores and raises an `AssertionError` if any of the named dimensions scores below its
minimum. Otherwise it does nothing. Requiring every dimension to be at least 95 passes here.
